fact: The National Association of Realtors' 2023 Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features estimates how much of the cost of 11 outdoor projects Realtors think a seller can recover at sale, from standard lawn care to an in-ground pool, and artificial turf is not one of the 11.
quote: The typical cost of 11 outdoor residential projects as estimated by members of the National Association of Landscape Professionals (NALP). … How much REALTORS® estimate homeowners can recover on the cost of the outdoor residential projects if they choose to sell the home … Cost Recovery On Outdoor Remodeling Projects Standard Lawn Care Service … Landscape Maintenance … Overall Landscape Upgrade … Outdoor Kitchen … New Patio … New Wood Deck … Tree Care … Irrigation System Installation … Landscape Lighting … Fire Feature … In-Ground Pool Addition
source_label: National Association of Realtors, 2023 Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features (PDF)
notes: Read the PDF (pdftotext) on 2026-09-25: the 11 projects are the ones listed in the quote; no artificial turf, synthetic turf or xeriscape project appears anywhere in the report. The report page (nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/research-reports/remodeling-impact-report-outdoor-features) links this PDF. NAR's 2025 Remodeling Impact report covers interior projects. The page does not reprint the cost-recovery percentages: none of them is about turf.

fact: In NAR's 2023 outdoor-features survey, 97% of Realtors said curb appeal is important in attracting a buyer when they work with a seller.
quote: When working with a residential seller, 97 percent of NAR members believe curb appeal is important in attracting a buyer (75 percent very important, 22 percent somewhat important).
source_label: National Association of Realtors, 2023 Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features (PDF)
notes: A survey of NAR members' opinions, not a measurement of sale prices. It says nothing about artificial turf.

fact: Colorado's standard Seller's Property Disclosure (Residential), SPD19, in mandatory use since January 1, 2026, is filled in to the seller's current actual knowledge, and a known adverse material fact must be disclosed whether or not the form has a line for it.
quote: SPD19 Seller’s Property Disclosure (Residential) Adoption Date: August 5, 2025 Mandatory Use Date: January 1, 2026 … Seller states that the information contained in this Seller’s Property Disclosure (“SPD”) is correct to Seller’s CURRENT ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE as of the date signed by Seller. … If Seller has knowledge of an adverse material fact affecting the Property or occupants, it must be disclosed whether there is a specific item on this SPD or not.
source_label: Colorado Real Estate Commission, SPD19 Seller's Property Disclosure (Residential), adopted August 5, 2025, mandatory use from January 1, 2026
notes: Read the fillable PDF linked from dre.colorado.gov/real-estate-broker-contracts-and-forms on 2026-09-25 (the site 403s plain curl; a browser user agent reads it, so reachable is false for manual re-checks). The form has no line that names artificial turf. The SPD is completed when the Contract to Buy and Sell requires it (the form's own words: "If the Contract to Buy and Sell (Contract) requires Seller to complete this SPD"); the 2026 CBS1 contract's § 10.1 refers to it. Re-check when the Commission adopts a new form.

fact: The SPD19 form asks the seller about violations of restrictive covenants or owners' association rules, improvements built in the past year without association approval, building code, city or county violations, and requirements for landscaping.
quote: L. USE, ZONING & LEGAL ISSUES If you know of any of the following EVER EXISTING, check the “Yes” column: … 5 Building code, city, or county violations 6 Violation of restrictive covenants or owners’ association rules or regulations 7 Any building or improvements constructed within the past one year before this Date without approval by the owner’s association or its designated approving body … 7 Requirements for curb, gravel/paving, or landscaping
source_label: Colorado Real Estate Commission, SPD19 Seller's Property Disclosure (Residential), Sections L.5 to L.7 and M.7
notes: L.5, L.6 and L.7 are under "Use, Zoning & Legal Issues"; the landscaping line is M.7 under "Access & Parking". The form also lists an underground sprinkler system (G.20) and irrigation system problems (G.28). Not legal advice: the page summarizes the form in two sentences and sends readers to their agent or a Colorado attorney.

fact: Greeley builds each single-family home's water budget from household size, the yard's irrigable square footage and real-time weather, allots 45 gallons a day per person indoors, sizes the outdoor budget to the yard, and asks customers to tell it when household size or irrigated area changes.
quote: A water budget consists of: Family size (number of people who live in the home) Landscape around the home (irrigable square footage of yard) Real-time weather conditions … Because each person in each household receives an allocation of 45 gallons per day, your indoor water budget will be twice as high as your neighbor's. But if your yard is half the size of your neighbor's, your outdoor water budget will be half the amount of your neighbor's. … How do I adjust my persons per household or irrigated area? Please let us know if anything needs to be corrected or has recently changed!
source_label: City of Greeley Water and Sewer, Budget Your Water (Water Budget Frequently Asked Questions)
notes: Read with curl on 2026-09-25; the FAQ answers sit in the page's accordion data. The page does not say whether artificial turf counts as irrigable area, so the guide tells a buyer to ask Greeley Water what area is on file. Rates per tier: greeley-water-budget-rates-2026.

fact: InterNACHI's home inspection standards say an inspection will not identify concealed defects or determine market value, and do not require the inspector to determine the service life or installation age of a component or code compliance, to research the property's history, or to inspect irrigation or sprinkler systems.
quote: An inspection will not identify concealed or latent defects. … An inspection does not determine the market value of the property or its marketability. … I. The inspector is not required to determine: … the service life expectancy of any component or system. … compliance with codes or regulations. … research the history of the property … determine the age of construction or installation of any system, structure or component of a building … inspect irrigation or sprinkler systems.
source_label: InterNACHI, International Standards of Practice for Performing a General Home Inspection, Sections 2.1, 2.2 and 3.2
notes: nachi.org returned 403 to curl and to WebFetch on 2026-09-25. Read in full from the Internet Archive capture of the same page dated 2026-09-13 (https://web.archive.org/web/20260913141456/https://www.nachi.org/sop.htm), hence EXTERNAL_SOURCE. Section 3.2 has the inspector inspect vegetation, surface drainage and grading only "where they may adversely affect the structure due to moisture intrusion". One association's standard; an inspector may offer more by agreement. Re-read on the live page in a browser.
